patients.summary: Kindergarten teacher who joins the practice healthy at 28, then develops celiac disease with iron deficiency anemia, osteopenia, restless legs and neuropathy, and later symptomatic uterine fibroids. Not seen since October 2025; in January 2026 she has a high-speed car crash with hemorrhagic shock and an emergency laparotomy, which reaches the practice only as late records.

documents.title: New Patient Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT — PREVENTIVE

28 y/o woman joining the practice. Teaches kindergarten at a public elementary school, started her fourth year this month. Had a PCP elsewhere through college and after; wants a doctor she can actually text. No active complaints today.

PMH: none she knows of. No hospitalizations.
PSH: none.
Meds: none. No supplements.
Allergies: NKDA.
OB/GYN: G0. Cycles regular. Last Pap per her report about a year ago, normal.
Family: mother — uterine fibroids. Sister — celiac disease. Maternal grandmother — osteoporosis. Father healthy as far as she knows.
Social: single, lives alone. Never smoked, no alcohol, no drugs. Walks and does a yoga class most weeks.

ROS: negative in full — no GI complaints, no weight change, energy fine.

Exam: well appearing, pleasant. HEENT normal, tongue normal. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart RRR without murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses. Skin without pallor. Neuro grossly normal. Mood bright.

PHQ-2: 0.

Assessment/Plan:
1. Adult preventive care. Tdap today (no record of one as an adult). CBC with baseline labs. Records request to prior office for Pap and vaccine history. Flu shot when available in the fall.
2. Family history of celiac in a first-degree relative noted. She has no symptoms; we discussed what to watch for (diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, fatigue) and that she should tell me if any of it shows up.

RTC one year for physical, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Records Request — Prior PCP
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Signed release on file. Request for last 3 years of records (visit notes, Pap, immunizations) faxed to previous primary care office.

documents.title: CBC Result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Blood count normal. Nothing to do. Sent to portal with a short note.

documents.title: Prior Primary Care Records
documents.author: outside primary care
documents.body:
Records from previous primary care office, 14 pages, covering 2015–2018.

Summary of contents:
- Annual visits 2015, 2016, 2017: healthy young woman, no chronic problems, no medications.
- Cervical cytology 2017: negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy.
- Immunizations: childhood series complete per state registry printout, including MMR x2 and varicella x2; HPV series completed as a teenager. Influenza most years.
- No known drug allergies.

Abstracted into chart by MA. Reviewed by PCP.

documents.title: Immunization — Influenza
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Came after school for flu vaccine. No fever today, no prior reactions. Quadrivalent 0.5 mL IM to left deltoid. VIS provided. Tolerated, left after brief wait.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL PHYSICAL

Juniper is here for her yearly visit, last week of the school year. Feels well. Sleeping fine. Periods regular, monthly, about five days, nothing unusual. Bowels normal. No weight change she has noticed.

Meds: none. NKDA.
Social: unchanged — teaching, lives alone, no tobacco or alcohol.

Exam: comfortable. Thyroid not enlarged. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear throughout. Abdomen soft, no tenderness or organomegaly. No pallor. Skin clear. Normal gait and strength.

PHQ-2 0.

Plan:
- One-time HIV and hepatitis C screening today, she agrees.
- CBC.
- Pap not due until 2020 (last 2017 normal); will do cotesting once she is 30.
- Flu vaccine in October.

Follow up in a year.

documents.title: Screening Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: HIV and hepatitis C screens nonreactive, blood count normal. Released to portal: 'All normal, Juniper. Enjoy the summer.'

documents.title: Immunization — Influenza
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Annual flu vaccine, quadrivalent 0.5 mL IM right deltoid. Afebrile, feels well. Mentioned her stomach has been 'off' since late summer and she will bring it up with the doctor; offered a visit, she will book after parent conferences. VIS given.

orders.order: DXA bone density, hip and spine
orders.reason: low body weight, family history of osteoporosis

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
OFFICE VISIT

CC: loose stools and bloating, losing weight.

HPI: Since about August she has had loose, frequent stools most days, 3–4 a day, with bloating and gas that make her uncomfortable by the end of the school day. Thinks it is worse after sandwiches or pasta but hasn't tested that. Weight down — her clothes are loose and the scale here confirms a big drop since June. Tired. For the last few weeks her tongue has been sore and red, hurts with hot or acidic food. No blood in stool, no black stools, no fever, no night sweats, no travel, no antibiotics. Periods unchanged.

FHx: sister with celiac disease.

Exam: thin, pale. BMI 18. Tongue smooth and red, tender. Mouth otherwise normal. Abdomen soft, mildly distended, hyperactive bowel sounds, no tenderness, no masses, no organomegaly. No lymphadenopathy. Heart and lungs normal.

A/P:
1. Chronic diarrhea with weight loss and glossitis, sister with celiac — celiac disease is high on the list; also considering other malabsorption. Labs today: CBC, BMP, TSH. Urgent GI referral; she'd prefer to have GI order the celiac serology and scope together, which is reasonable — asked her NOT to start a gluten-free diet before GI sees her.
2. Low body weight, grandmother with osteoporosis — DXA ordered.
3. Will call with results.

Time spent including counseling: 35 minutes.

documents.title: Referral Scheduling
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Outside GI group called back with first available new patient slot early February. Put her on their cancellation list. Pt notified by phone.

documents.title: Lab Result Call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called Juniper at lunch. Hemoglobin 10.3 with small red cells — a new anemia since June. With the diarrhea this most likely fits malabsorption; GI will check iron studies and the celiac blood test with the rest of their workup. Kidney function, electrolytes and thyroid normal. She'll keep eating normally until GI sees her. Call if any blood in stool, fainting or worsening.

reports.study: DXA bone density, hip and spine
reports.text:
EXAM: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, lumbar spine and left hip.
INDICATION: 30-year-old woman (age 30 at study) with low body weight and family history of osteoporosis.
TECHNIQUE: Standard acquisition on a fan-beam densitometer. L1–L4 analyzed; no vertebrae excluded. Left proximal femur.
FINDINGS:
Lumbar spine L1–L4: BMD 0.871 g/cm2. T-score -1.7. Z-score -1.6.
Left femoral neck: BMD 0.715 g/cm2. T-score -1.4. Z-score -1.3.
Left total hip: T-score -1.1.
No prior study for comparison.
reports.conclusion: Low bone mass (osteopenia range) at the lumbar spine and femoral neck. In a premenopausal woman, Z-scores are preferred; secondary causes should be considered clinically.

documents.title: DXA Bone Density Report
documents.author: radiology
documents.body: Bone density study of 2020-01-07: lumbar spine T -1.7 / Z -1.6; left femoral neck T -1.4 / Z -1.3. Impression: low bone mass, osteopenia range. Consider evaluation for secondary causes in a premenopausal patient.

medications.drug_text: calcium carbonate 1500 MG / cholecalciferol 400 UNT Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily with food

documents.title: DXA Result Call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Reviewed bone density with Juniper by phone. Thinner bones than expected for 30 — the osteopenia range. Most likely tied to whatever is going on with her gut (poor absorption, low weight); GI visit is next month. Start calcium 600 mg with vitamin D 400 units twice a day with food, sent to her pharmacy. Weight-bearing exercise, which she already does. We'll recheck bone density in a few years.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY — NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 2020-02-03
Referred by: primary care

Thank you for sending Ms. Nakamura, a 30-year-old teacher, seen for half a year of loose stools, bloating and weight loss with a painful tongue.

She describes stools that are loose and frequent, with abdominal distention that builds over the day. She has noticed she feels worse after bread or pasta. She is fatigued. She points to a smooth, sore, reddened area on the tongue. Her primary care physician recently obtained a bone density study showing osteopenia; she is now on calcium with vitamin D.

PMH: osteopenia (DXA January 2020). Microcytic anemia on recent primary care labs.
PSH: none.
Medications: calcium carbonate 600 mg / vitamin D3 400 units twice daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: sister with celiac disease; mother with fibroids; maternal grandmother with osteoporosis.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol. Elementary school teacher.

Exam: pale, thin young woman. BMI 18. Atrophic glossitis. Abdomen soft, mildly distended, not tender. Neurologic: sensation diminished to the wrists and mid-shins in a stocking-glove pattern; strength normal.

Labs drawn here today: hemoglobin 10 g/dL, MCV 74 fL, iron 30 ug/dL, TIBC 400 ug/dL, ferritin 15 ng/mL, calcium 8.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 120 U/L. Tissue transglutaminase IgA sent, result to follow.

Impression: chronic diarrhea with weight loss, iron-poor microcytic anemia, low calcium and glossitis in a patient with a sister with celiac disease. Celiac disease is the leading consideration. The sensory findings may reflect nutritional deficiency.

Plan:
1. Await tTG-IgA.
2. Upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies — she should keep eating gluten until then.
3. If confirmed, gluten-free diet with dietitian teaching.
4. Iron repletion and bone health to be followed with her primary care physician.

We will send results as they return.

documents.title: GI Result Note — Celiac Serology
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body: FYI to primary care. Tissue transglutaminase IgA from 2/3/2020: 96 U/mL (reference <4). Strongly positive. EGD with duodenal biopsies scheduled for 2/26. Patient informed and asked to continue a normal diet until the procedure.

reports.text:
SPECIMEN: Duodenum, bulb and second portion, cold forceps biopsies (6 fragments).
GROSS: Multiple tan-pink soft tissue fragments, 0.2–0.3 cm, entirely submitted.
MICROSCOPIC: Duodenal mucosa with total villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia and marked increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes (more than 40 per 100 enterocytes). Lamina propria with increased plasma cells. No granulomas, no dysplasia, no organisms identified.
reports.conclusion: Duodenum, biopsies: villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh 3), consistent with celiac disease in the setting of positive serology.

documents.title: Upper Endoscopy Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
ENDOSCOPY REPORT — date of procedure 2020-02-26
Procedure: esophagogastroduodenoscopy with biopsy.
Indication: positive tTG-IgA, chronic diarrhea, iron deficiency.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care. Tolerated well.
Findings: Esophagus normal. Stomach normal. Duodenal bulb and second portion with scalloped folds and a mosaic mucosal pattern. Biopsies x6 taken from bulb and distal duodenum.
Complications: none.
Impression: duodenal appearance suggestive of celiac disease; await pathology.

ADDENDUM (pathology): Marsh 3 villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Diagnosis: celiac disease. Plan: strict gluten-free diet, dietitian visit arranged, repeat tTG in about 6 months. Primary care to follow anemia and bone health.

documents.title: Celiac Confirmation Reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: GI scope and biopsies confirm celiac disease. Added to problem list. Portal message to Juniper: 'This confirms celiac. The gluten-free diet is the treatment and most people feel much better within a few months. Let's do a video visit in April to see how it's going.'

procedures.procedure: Telehealth visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Video Visit — Celiac Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit from her kitchen; identity checked with date of birth. She is teaching her class over video from home and finds it exhausting but manageable.

Strictly gluten-free since early March after the dietitian session; reads labels, replaced her toaster, eats at home. Stools now formed most days, bloating much better. Tongue no longer sore. Weight up by her bathroom scale. Still tired in the afternoons.

Taking calcium/vitamin D twice daily.

Assessment: celiac disease, early good response to diet. Osteopenia on calcium/D.
Plan: office visit with labs in the summer when the office reopens to routine visits — blood count, iron, tTG. Keep going.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth three times daily

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
OFFICE VISIT — in person, masked.

CC: tired for months, woozy when she stands up fast.

HPI: Six months now of fatigue — gets winded and worn out walking short distances or climbing the stairs to her classroom, which wasn't true a year ago. Brief lightheadedness if she pops up from the floor with the kids or out of bed. No fainting. Appetite good. GI symptoms have resolved on the gluten-free diet: no diarrhea, no change in bowel habits, no further weight loss — in fact weight is back up. No recent illness. Eats mixed meals including meat; not vegetarian. Periods every 28 days, 5 days, moderate flow, some cramps. No melena, no bright red blood, no blood in urine, no other bleeding.

G0. Calcium/vitamin D twice daily — the only thing she takes.

ROS otherwise negative; thinking, vision and mood all fine.

Exam: BMI 23. Looks well, a bit pale. Conjunctival pallor. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no liver or spleen edge, no masses. No cervical, axillary or inguinal nodes. Neuro: intact today.

A/P:
1. Iron deficiency anemia — persistent microcytic anemia with low iron stores (GI's February iron studies; repeat today). Cause is malabsorption from celiac; menstrual losses sound modest. Start ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily; take with orange juice or vitamin C, separate from calcium by 2 hours. Counseled on dark stools and constipation.
2. Celiac disease — doing well on diet. tTG today. Start a daily gluten-free multivitamin.
3. Osteopenia — continue calcium/D.
4. Orthostatic lightheadedness likely from anemia; fluids, rise slowly.

Recheck CBC and iron in about 3 months.

documents.title: Iron Instructions
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg: one tablet three times a day. Take with a little vitamin C (juice is fine). Keep it 2 hours away from your calcium and from tea or coffee. Stools will turn dark — that is expected. If your stomach rebels, call and we can adjust. Daily multivitamin: choose one labeled gluten-free.

documents.title: Your Lab Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Juniper — hemoglobin 10.4, ferritin 11: still low on iron, which fits how tired you feel, so the iron pills are the right move. The celiac antibody has come down from 96 to 41, a real improvement on the diet. Kidney and liver tests fine; calcium on the low side of normal. Let's recheck the blood count in October.

documents.title: Re: Your Lab Results
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thank you! Glad the number is going down. Started the iron yesterday, so far so good. See you in the fall.

documents.title: Nurse Visit — Flu Vaccine and Lab Draw
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Screened at door, no COVID symptoms. Blood drawn for CBC and iron studies per PCP. Flu vaccine 0.5 mL IM left deltoid, VIS reviewed. Reports taking iron three times daily most days; occasionally misses the midday dose at school.

documents.title: CBC and Iron Reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hgb 10.6, ferritin 13. Barely moved after nearly 3 months of oral iron. Asked front desk to book her for an in-person visit next month to talk about next steps.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

orders.reason: iron deficiency anemia not responding to oral iron

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up of anemia.

On ferrous sulfate three times daily since late July, misses the occasional midday dose. Some dark stools, mild nausea if she takes it on an empty stomach. Still tired. Gluten-free diet strict. Since September she has stopped eating meat and eats vegetarian, mostly beans, eggs, dairy, rice and gluten-free grains. Periods unchanged by her account.

October labs: hemoglobin 10.6, ferritin 13 — little response.

Exam: pale conjunctivae. Heart regular. Abdomen benign. Weight steady.

A/P: Iron deficiency anemia with poor response to oral iron in a patient with celiac disease (absorption) and now a vegetarian diet. Referring to hematology to weigh further evaluation and options. Continue oral iron, take with food if nauseated. Celiac — stable, tTG due in spring.

documents.title: Hematology Consultation
documents.author: hematology
documents.body:
HEMATOLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 2021-01-22
Reason for referral: iron deficiency anemia with limited response to oral iron.

Ms. Nakamura is a 31-year-old elementary school teacher with celiac disease (2020) and iron deficiency anemia (July 2020). The main thing she wanted to discuss today is her sleep, which has been broken for several months. When she lies down at night, particularly while resting quietly or watching TV, she gets a strong, unpleasant need to move her legs — a crawling feeling deep in the calves that is not painful but very irritating. Moving relieves it, so she gets up and walks around until it passes. It is an evening and night problem; daytime is free of it. She is tired during the day and blames the poor sleep. No snoring, choking or witnessed pauses in breathing.

Menses are regular but heavy, lasting 6 to 7 days.

Medications: ferrous sulfate 325 mg TID, multivitamin daily, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3 BID.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: sister with celiac disease, mother with uterine fibroids, maternal grandmother with osteoporosis.
Social: teaches, exercises regularly, vegetarian diet, no alcohol, no drugs.

Exam: BMI 22. Unremarkable general exam. No neurologic deficit; normal tone and strength. Legs without edema; pulses and skin normal.

No sleep study has been done.

Assessment:
1. Restless legs syndrome — clinical diagnosis by the standard criteria; iron deficiency is a known contributor.
2. Iron deficiency anemia with ongoing heavy menstrual losses (menorrhagia) and celiac malabsorption.

Recommendations:
- Continue oral iron as prescribed.
- Sleep hygiene; avoid caffeine late in the day.
- Follow up here in six months.

Thank you for this referral.

documents.title: Call Re: Hematology Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Spoke with Juniper about the hematology consult. Restless legs and heavy periods now on her problem list. Hematology wants her to stay on oral iron; she will try to be more consistent with the midday dose by keeping a bottle in her desk. Follow-up visit with me in May.

documents.title: Vaccine Card
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi! Got both Pfizer shots through the educator clinic at a pharmacy — March 20 and April 10. Photo of my card attached. Sore arm and a tired day after the second one, fine now.

documents.title: Re: Vaccine Card
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Thanks Juniper, both doses entered in your immunization record.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Routine follow-up. Back in the classroom full time. Saw hematology in January — note reviewed: restless legs, keep oral iron, sleep habits. Legs still bother her most nights; she stretches and walks laps of the apartment. Periods heavy as before. Bowels fine. Vaccinated for COVID.

Meds: ferrous sulfate TID, MVI, calcium/D BID. Taking them.

Exam: mild pallor. Heart RRR. Lungs clear. Abd soft.

A/P: iron deficiency anemia on oral iron, RLS, menorrhagia, celiac on GFD, osteopenia. Labs today. Hematology follow-up is due in July — she has it booked.

documents.title: Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hgb 10.2, ferritin 12, tTG 22 (continuing down). Portal note sent; she will discuss iron with hematology in July.

reports.text: Specimen: liquid-based cervical cytology with high-risk HPV testing. Specimen adequacy: satisfactory for evaluation; transformation zone component present. Interpretation: negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. High-risk HPV: not detected.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
PHYSICAL

Second week of school. She saw hematology in July and says they found her blood count lower and that she has numbness in her hands and feet; she has also lost weight over the summer and had some loose stools again. We have not received that note — requesting it today. She isn't sure what the plan was beyond staying on iron.

Legs still restless at night. Periods heavy.

Meds: ferrous sulfate TID, MVI, calcium/D BID.

Exam: weight down about 4.5 kg since January. Pale. Thyroid normal. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Pelvic: normal external genitalia, cervix normal, Pap with HPV collected. Skin normal.

PHQ-2: 1.

Plan: Pap/HPV sent. CBC, CMP. Hematology note requested. Flu shot next month at nurse visit. Will reach out once the hematology letter is in.

documents.title: Records Request — Hematology
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Faxed request to outside hematology for July 2021 visit note and labs.

documents.title: Hematology Follow-up
documents.author: hematology
documents.body:
HEMATOLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Date of service: 2021-07-26
(sent at request of primary care)

Returning patient with celiac disease, iron deficiency anemia and restless legs syndrome. Over the past 6 months: fatigue, intermittent diarrhea, and more recently numbness and tingling in both hands and feet. She has lost 10 pounds over 3 months with no change in what she eats or how much she exercises. Anemia has not corrected on oral iron.

Medications: ferrous sulfate 325 mg TID, multivitamin, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3 BID.
Allergies: none known.

Exam: pallor. Abdomen mildly distended, nontender. Light-touch sensation reduced in a stocking-glove distribution.

Labs: Hgb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 74 fL, serum iron 30 ug/dL, TIBC 450 ug/dL, calcium 8.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 120 U/L, intact PTH 92 pg/mL (ref 15-65).

Assessment: iron deficiency anemia refractory to oral iron; peripheral neuropathy; low calcium with raised PTH.

Plan: continue ferrous sulfate. Return in 6 months.

documents.title: Hematology Letter Reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: July hematology letter reviewed. Peripheral neuropathy added to problem list. Plan per hematology is to continue oral iron. Copy to portal.

documents.title: Immunization — Influenza
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Influenza quadrivalent 0.5 mL IM, left arm. No contraindications. VIS given. Plans COVID booster at her pharmacy next month.

documents.title: Booster
documents.author: patient
documents.body:
Got my booster Saturday at the pharmacy (Pfizer). Could you add it?

Also — the leg thing at night is getting old. Some nights it's 1am before I can stay in bed. Can we talk about it?

documents.title: Re: Booster
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Booster added. Yes — let's do a video visit in the next couple of weeks about the restless legs. The front desk will reach out.

documents.title: Video Visit — Restless Legs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video from home after school.

Restless legs since about a year and a half ago, diagnosed by hematology in January. Evening urge to move, eased by walking, keeps her up most nights. Tried stretching, warm baths, no caffeine after noon. Still on iron TID; ferritin has stayed low.

No snoring or witnessed apneas.

Assessment: restless legs syndrome with significant sleep disruption despite iron and sleep measures.
Plan: neurology referral for treatment options; she prefers a video consult if they offer one. Keep iron going.

medications.sig: Take 1 capsule by mouth at bedtime

documents.title: Neurology Telehealth Consultation
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
NEUROLOGY — TELEHEALTH VISIT
Date of service: 2022-01-17
Visit by secure video; patient at home.

32-year-old woman with celiac disease and iron deficiency anemia, referred for restless legs first evaluated in January 2021. For several months the symptoms have been steady: in the evening she feels a deep, crawling discomfort in both legs with an irresistible need to move them, relieved only while she is moving. She gets out of bed and walks, which pushes back her sleep, and she is tired the following day. Nothing during the day; worst lying down at night. No snoring, gasping or observed apneas.

She eats a vegetarian diet. Menses are heavy, 6 to 7 days.

Medications: ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily, multivitamin, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3.
Allergies: none.

Exam (video): alert, fluent, cranial nerves grossly normal, moves all limbs symmetrically, normal finger-nose and gait as observed. Neurologic examination normal within the limits of video.

Assessment: restless legs syndrome, persistent, in the setting of iron deficiency.

Plan:
- Start gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime.
- Continue iron; ideally ferritin above 75 for RLS.
- Check in by phone in two weeks.

documents.title: Neurology Addendum
documents.author: neurology
documents.body: Telephone follow-up 2022-01-31: two weeks into gabapentin 300 mg nightly. Partial relief — falls asleep sooner on most nights, still some evenings with symptoms. Mild morning grogginess the first few days, now gone. Continue current dose. Return as needed or in 6 months.

documents.title: Neurology Notes Reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Gabapentin 300 mg qhs added to med list as started by neurology. Partial benefit at two weeks.

documents.title: Gabapentin Refill Request
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Pharmacy refill request for gabapentin 300 mg capsules, #30. Original Rx from outside neurology. Pt asks if PCP can manage refills going forward. Routed to PCP.

documents.title: Gabapentin Refill — Approved
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: OK to refill gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime, #90 with 3 refills. We'll manage going forward.

documents.title: Iron Recheck
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Neurology suggested aiming for a ferritin above 75 for her legs. Ferritin 13, hemoglobin 10.4 on oral iron TID. Message to patient: keep taking it consistently; we'll go over it at the May visit.

documents.title: Re: Iron Recheck
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Ugh, OK. I really am taking them! See you in May.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up.

RLS: gabapentin at bedtime helps — she's asleep within half an hour most nights now, maybe two bad nights a week. No daytime sedation.
GI: stools normal again since the fall; strict about cross-contamination at school lunches. Weight coming back up.
Iron: TID, tolerating. Periods still heavy and long.
Numbness in feet comes and goes, mild.

Exam: BP fine. Pale conjunctivae. Heart RRR, lungs clear. Feet: light touch slightly reduced at the toes bilaterally, strength normal.

A/P:
1. IDA — labs today.
2. Celiac on GFD — tTG today.
3. RLS — continue gabapentin 300 qhs.
4. Neuropathy — stable, mild.
5. Osteopenia — calcium/D.
Physical in September.

documents.title: Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hgb 10.5, ferritin 14, tTG 9 — continuing to fall. Portal message sent.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL

Good summer — gardened, swam. Feels steadier than last year. Sleep decent on gabapentin. No GI flares. Periods heavy, she is used to them.

Meds: ferrous sulfate 325 TID, gabapentin 300 qhs, MVI, calcium carbonate/D3 BID.
NKDA.

Exam: well. Thyroid normal. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Mild conjunctival pallor. Skin normal. Feet: mild distal light-touch reduction, unchanged.

PHQ-2: 0.

Prevention: Pap/HPV 2021 negative — next 2026. Flu and bivalent COVID booster today.

Labs: CBC, CMP.

documents.title: Missed Tuesday
documents.author: patient
documents.body: So sorry — I completely forgot Tuesday's appointment, we had a staff meeting run late. Can I come in the spring instead? Also could you send a new iron prescription, I'm on my last bottle.

documents.title: Re: Missed Tuesday
documents.author: MA
documents.body: No problem. You're booked for May. Ferrous sulfate refill sent to your pharmacy.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Rescheduled from November.

Doing well overall. GFD strict. Legs controlled most nights on gabapentin. Iron TID. Feet tingle now and then. Periods heavy, 6–7 days, same as before.

Exam: mild pallor. Heart, lungs normal. Abdomen soft.

Plan: CBC, iron studies, tTG. Continue all meds. Physical in the fall.

documents.title: Results

documents.body: tTG now 3 — in the normal range for the first time. Hgb 10.3, ferritin 12, unchanged. Portal message: 'Your celiac antibody is finally normal — great work on the diet. Iron is about where it has been.'

Since about the summer her periods have become heavier and longer — now more than a week, soaking through pads quickly on the heavy days. She also has a sense of fullness or pressure low in the pelvis, and has been running to the bathroom more and a bit constipated. Mother had fibroids.

Exam: abdomen soft, nontender; lower abdomen feels full above the pubis, hard to define on exam. Pelvic deferred to gynecology at her request.

A/P: worsening heavy menstrual bleeding with pelvic pressure; family history of fibroids. Gynecology referral for evaluation and pelvic imaging. Continue iron.

reports.text:
TECHNIQUE: Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound.
FINDINGS: Uterus enlarged with a lobulated contour. Multiple well-circumscribed hypoechoic masses within the myometrium, the largest measuring 5.0 cm. Posterior aspect of the uterus partly beyond the transvaginal field of view. Endometrium not distorted where seen. Both ovaries normal in size and appearance. No free fluid.

documents.title: Gynecology Consultation
documents.author: gynecology
documents.body:
GYNECOLOGY NEW PATIENT CONSULT
Visit date: 2024-01-15

Referred by primary care for worsening menstrual bleeding.

Ms. Nakamura is 34, G0. Over the last 6 months her menses have grown heavy and prolonged — 8 to 10 days, changing pads about every 2 hours on the heaviest days — with a sense of pelvic pressure. She also notes urinary frequency and constipation, which she connects to the pressure. Iron deficiency anemia, diagnosed by her internist in 2020, on oral iron; celiac disease followed by GI.

Meds: ferrous sulfate 325 mg TID, multivitamin, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3 BID.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family: mother had uterine fibroids; sister celiac; maternal grandmother osteoporosis.

Exam: abdomen soft, nontender. A firm, irregular lower abdominal mass is palpable, in keeping with an enlarged uterus. Bimanual: enlarged irregular uterus, mobile, nontender. Adnexa not separately felt.

Labs: Hgb 10.2 g/dL, ferritin 15 ng/mL, platelets 250,000, PT 12 s, aPTT 30 s.

Ultrasound (TV): several well-circumscribed hypoechoic intramyometrial masses, largest 5 cm.

Impression: symptomatic uterine leiomyomas with heavy menstrual bleeding; iron deficiency anemia. Coagulation normal.

Plan: options reviewed in general terms (medical therapy, procedures, surgery). She would like time to think. Continue iron. Return in 6 months, sooner if bleeding worsens.

documents.title: Gynecology Letter Reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Fibroids confirmed on ultrasound, largest 5 cm. Added uterine leiomyoma to problem list. Gyn follow-up in July.

reports.text:
TECHNIQUE: Transabdominal and transvaginal pelvic ultrasound. Comparison: transvaginal study 2024-01-15.
FINDINGS: Enlarged uterus. Subserosal fibroid of the posterior uterine wall measuring 10 cm, larger than on the prior transvaginal study, where it was incompletely seen. Pedunculated fibroid arising from the anterior wall measuring 5 cm. Endometrial stripe normal in thickness. Ovaries normal. No free fluid. Kidneys without hydronephrosis.
reports.conclusion: Posterior subserosal fibroid 10 cm and anterior pedunculated fibroid 5 cm. Normal endometrial stripe.

GYNECOLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Visit date: 2024-07-15

She returns with fibroids, iron deficiency anemia and celiac disease. For 6 months she has felt pelvic pressure and as if she does not fully empty her bladder. Over the past year, flow has been heavier and lasts longer; cycles remain regular. No urinary leakage, no painful urination. Never pregnant; not currently sexually active.

Meds: ferrous sulfate 325 mg TID, multivitamin, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3 BID.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: abdomen nontender; a pelvic mass rises to the level of the umbilicus.

Labs: Hgb 10.2 g/dL, Hct 30.5%, MCV 78 fL, ferritin 15 ng/mL.

Ultrasound (TA and TV): 10 cm subserosal fibroid, posterior wall; 5 cm pedunculated fibroid, anterior wall; endometrial stripe normal.

Assessment: symptomatic uterine leiomyomas with bulk symptoms and heavy menstrual bleeding; anemia.

Plan:
- Abdominal myomectomy discussed, including risks and recovery. She prefers to defer surgery for now and will let us know when she is ready.
- Tranexamic acid 1300 mg three times daily for up to 5 days with each period.
- Continue oral iron.
- Repeat ultrasound in one year or sooner with symptoms.

reports.text:
INDICATION: high-speed motor vehicle collision, post-operative.
TECHNIQUE: Axial noncontrast CT of the head.
FINDINGS: No intracranial hemorrhage, mass effect or midline shift. Gray-white differentiation preserved. Ventricles and sulci normal for age. No calvarial fracture. Visualized paranasal sinuses and mastoids clear.
Portable AP chest, trauma bay. Lungs clear. No pneumothorax. No pleural effusion. Mediastinum not widened. No displaced rib fracture.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT — TRAUMA
Arrival: 2026-01-18 16:40, by ambulance.

36-year-old woman, restrained driver in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. On arrival alert but pale and anxious, complaining of abdominal pain and dizziness. History per patient and EMS: iron deficiency anemia, uterine fibroids, celiac disease, restless legs, osteopenia, heavy periods. Home meds per patient: ferrous sulfate 325 mg TID, multivitamin, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3. No known drug allergies. No prior surgery.

Primary survey: airway patent, breath sounds equal. BP 90/60, HR 120, RR 22. GCS 15.
Abdomen distended, tender throughout all four quadrants with guarding.

Labs: Hgb 7 g/dL, Hct 21%, platelets 250,000, PT 12 s, PTT 30 s. Type and crossmatch sent, blood type pending.
FAST: free fluid in the abdomen.
Portable chest and pelvis films: no acute traumatic findings.

Assessment: hemorrhagic shock from intra-abdominal bleeding after blunt trauma.

Course: two large-bore IVs. Emergency-release O-negative red cells started in the bay; massive transfusion protocol activated. Trauma surgery at bedside; taken directly to the operating room at 17:35.

documents.title: Operative Report — Exploratory Laparotomy
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT
Date of surgery: 2026-01-18
Preoperative diagnosis: hemorrhagic shock, blunt abdominal trauma, positive FAST.
Postoperative diagnosis: small-bowel mesenteric laceration with active hemorrhage; traumatic hemorrhagic shock with acute coagulopathy.
Procedure: exploratory laparotomy, suture ligation of mesenteric bleeding vessel, repair of mesenteric laceration.
Anesthesia: general endotracheal.

Findings: approximately 1.5 L of hemoperitoneum. Laceration of the small-bowel mesentery with an actively bleeding mesenteric vessel. Bowel viable throughout after hemostasis; no resection required. Liver, spleen, stomach, colon, kidneys and retroperitoneum without injury. Enlarged fibroid uterus noted, not injured. Diffuse oozing from raw surfaces during the case; INR 1.7, fibrinogen 130 mg/dL on intraoperative labs.

Description: midline laparotomy, four-quadrant packing, systematic exploration. Bleeding mesenteric vessel suture-ligated; mesenteric defect closed. Small bowel run twice from ligament to ileocecal valve. Oozing treated with plasma and cryoprecipitate with improvement. Fascia closed, skin stapled.

Resuscitation totals: 6 units packed red cells, 4 units plasma, 1 apheresis platelet unit, 1 pooled cryoprecipitate dose.
EBL: see anesthesia record. Specimens: none. Complications: none apparent.
Disposition: surgical ICU, intubated, then extubated the same night.

Blood type resulted O positive.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 2026-01-18. Discharged: 2026-01-23.

Discharge diagnoses:
1. Traumatic hemorrhagic shock with acute coagulopathy after high-speed motor vehicle collision.
2. Laceration of small-bowel mesentery, status post exploratory laparotomy with suture ligation and repair 1/18.
Chronic: iron deficiency anemia, celiac disease, uterine leiomyoma, restless legs syndrome, osteopenia, menorrhagia.

Hospital course: Arrived in hemorrhagic shock with positive FAST; emergency-release O-negative blood and massive transfusion protocol, then emergency laparotomy (see operative report). Intraoperative coagulopathy (INR 1.7, fibrinogen 130) corrected with plasma and cryoprecipitate. Total 6 u PRBC, 4 u plasma, 1 apheresis platelet unit, 1 pooled cryoprecipitate dose. Extubated post-op night. Tertiary survey and post-operative CT head and cervical spine without contrast: no further injury. Chest and pelvis films normal. Diet advanced, bowel function returned, ambulating independently. Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL on day of discharge, stable.

Discharge medications:
- Oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain, 5 days.
- Acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours.
- Resume home ferrous sulfate, multivitamin, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3.

Follow-up: trauma surgery clinic in 2 weeks for staple removal and wound check. Primary care in 1–2 weeks.
Activity: no lifting over 10 lb for 6 weeks. No driving while taking oxycodone.
